newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Disarmament negotiators blocked on agenda for 1997.
newsitem.headline: Disarmament negotiators blocked on agenda for 1997.

text.p: Negotiators from 61 countries meet this week to launch the 1997 session of the United Nations-sponsored Conference on Disarmament (CD) -- but they have yet to agree on what to talk about.

After weeks of informal discussion, key diplomats said the CD was in "temporary paralysis" amid demands from developing states that total nuclear disarmament should be the top priority and a refusal by the big powers to agree.
"It could take weeks yet before we decide which direction work is going to go this year," said one envoy. "Positions on both sides seem very firm and there is no obvious quick fix."

The CD, launched in 1979 as the main world forum on reducing the vast stocks of weaponry of all types held around the globe, marked up a success last year by completing a treaty banning all nuclear weapons tests, the CTBT.

But the two years of negotiation provided a foretaste of the impasse that now looms, as the pact was only finalised through a procedural manouevre outflanking India, which argued it should be firmly tied to a commitment to overall nuclear disarmament.

Although other developing countries went along with the action -- taking the CTBT text to the U.N. General Assembly where majority voting is the rule rather than the consensus required in the CD -- they have now rallied round India.

Diplomats say the so-called Group of 21 in the CD, which also includes India's potential nuclear rival Pakistan, Iran and South Africa, is insisting nothing can be done before agreement on tackling the nuclear weapons issue.

The Group is seeking creation of a committee with a firm mandate to begin preparation of the text of a treaty that would totally ban nuclear weapons and set a strict timeframe for the destruction of stockpiles.

The five declared nuclear powers -- the United States, Russia, China, Britain and France -- argue that nuclear disarmament is best handled through bilateral and multilateral negotiations and agreements between them.
All five say the CD should focus attention now on negotiating a pact setting a date for a cut-off in production of the fissile material used in nuclear weapons (FMCT) as a follow-up to the CTBT.

Britain, France and now the United States, which formally joined its Western allies on the issue at the weekend, also want discussion of elimination of production and sale on anti-personnel landmines to be put on the agenda.
The G-21 states say they are ready for talks on both, but only once nuclear disarmament treaty negotiations are set up.

Not all Western countries agree that the CD would be the best framework for a bid to ban landmines, some 100 million of which are laid around the globe and which kill or maim some 25,000 people, mainly civilians, a year.

Last October, at the initiative of Canada which has taken a lead on the problem, some 50 countries -- including the United States, France, Britain, Japan and Iran -- met in Ottawa and issued a declaration calling for an early ban.
Canada proposed immediate negotiations with the aim of having a text ready for another conference in Ottawa at the end of this year when it could be signed.

But Russia and China, the two main producers and exporters of mines, have stood aloof from the process, arguing that for the present there is no alternative. Western diplomats say both have, however, indicated they would accept CD talks.
